item.title: Nuclear power connected to national grid for the first time
item.description:
For the first time in the country's history, nuclear power has been connected to the national grid.

This means that the process of supplying electricity from the first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant to the national grid has begun on an experimental basis.

However, the power plant is not yet going into commercial production. Electricity is being supplied to the grid primarily for testing and experimentation purposes.

The supply of 350 megawatts of nuclear power from Rooppur to the national grid began today, Tuesday, at 3:6 PM.

Posts, Telecommunications, and Information Technology minister Fakir Mahbub Anam was present.

After a long wait, continuous technical activities, and complex tests at various stages, electricity produced from Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant at Rooppur has been experimentally connected to the national grid.

The information has been confirmed through an instant press release sent from the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant construction project. It states that, under primary trial connection, electricity will be supplied to the national grid for approximately 8 to 10 hours.

During this period, key technical tests, including the effectiveness and stability of the integrated operational system with the power plant's turbine, generator, and grid, will be conducted.

Subsequently, the power plant will be disconnected from the national grid for various technical tests. After a break of about 28 hours, it will be reconnected to the grid for 4 to 6 hours to complete the necessary technical and operational tests.

According to sources at the Rooppur power plant, today marks the initiation of the trial phase to gradually increase power production capability following the guidelines and standards of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Now, following the design and regulatory conditions, approximately 350 megawatts of electricity from the power plant's first unit will be supplied to the national grid for a few hours.

After the commencement of power supply, the functionality of various equipment including the nuclear reactor vessel, turbine, generator, and automated control systems will be tested.

For these tests, the first unit may be temporarily shut down at various times, and the production and supply of electricity may be reduced or increased. However, customers will be able to use the supplied electricity to the grid throughout the period.

Sources from the nuclear power plant state that it will not be possible to ensure uninterrupted and stable electricity supply to the national grid during the trial period. The Power Grid Company of Bangladesh (PGCB) will take necessary measures to maintain the balance of the national grid, considering the temporary shutdown of Rooppur power plant's first unit and the fluctuation of electricity supply.

Officials from the Power Development Board (PDB) will also monitor the supply situation.

Necessary licenses and approvals must be obtained from the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) to gradually enhance production capacity to 100 per cent.

Therefore, following the tests, the report of results will be submitted to BAERA by the Rooppur authorities. Upon their approval, the process of increasing capacity will begin, along with the test supply to the grid.

It may take several months for the power production capacity to gradually reach 100 per cent.

According to the agreement with the Russian contractor, after completing a 10-month trial operation, electricity will be supplied commercially from the first unit at full capacity permanently.

Power plant officials state that the trial production may continue for several months continuously after initiation. However, with electricity reaching the grid, Bangladesh has become the 33rd country in the world in the list of nuclear electricity-producing countries.

Although the formal recognition will come when the full-fledged supply starts after testing. Earlier, in October 2023, the Rooppur power plant was recognised as a nuclear facility after the arrival of nuclear fuel in the project area. With the receipt of the fuel, Bangladesh has been enlisted as a nuclear power-holding country.

The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant is the largest single project in the country's history. The project is being implemented by the Atomic Energy Commission under the Ministry of Science and Technology. The project is managed by a government company named Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Limited (NPCBL). Russia's contractor Atomstroyexport is constructing two units of 1,200 megawatts each in Rooppur.

The Rooppur project's duration was until December 2025. The duration has been extended twice, now up to June 2028.

Despite the extension of the duration as per the contract with the contractor, there is no opportunity to increase the project's cost.

However, due to the increase in the dollar rate, the project cost has increased by Tk 260 billion. The Rooppur power plant will cost Tk 1,386.86 billion.

item.title: “Choked by design”: How small, low bridges killing rivers in Bangladesh
item.description:
Beyond Aminbazar in Savar, along the Dhaka–Aricha Highway, stands Salehpur Bridge over the Turag River. The approach roads at both ends of the bridge extend far into the river’s boundaries. At the foot of the bridge, the river is struggling to flow through what has become a narrow canal.

On 6 August, a walk along the site revealed that the approach roads encroaching on the river stretched for a total of 160 paces, or approximately 250 feet. This means that at least that much of the river’s width has been filled in across the two ends.

Seen from above through a drone, it looks as though someone has squeezed the river in their fist. The bridge has been shortened to just 59 paces, while silt is accumulating upstream and gradually filling the river. Downstream of the bridge, the river widens again as it flows towards the Buriganga.

Kanu Mia, a resident of Salehpur village, fishes in those waters. Standing on the bank, the elderly man said, “Ever since the bridge was built, the river has become narrower. They have killed the river here with this bridge.”

Signs of the river’s death are clear on one side of the bridge. There, houses and brick kilns have sprung up on land reclaimed from the river, which has been filled with silt and rubbish.

Salehpur is not alone. Across the country, bridge after bridge built without following rules and regulations and by encroaching on rivers has become a noose around rivers’ necks.

AKM Saiful Islam is a professor at the Institute of Water and Flood Management at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET). He told Prothom Alo that when approach roads are extended into a river’s main channel to reduce the length of a bridge, they severely obstruct the flow of water through the narrowed river.

According to him, this causes two kinds of damage. First, silt gets trapped upstream, gradually filling the river. Second, as water rushes through the narrowed section downstream, it erodes the riverbed and causes the banks to collapse.

The expert added that obstructing the natural flow in this way can sometimes effectively kill a river. It also damages the floodplains along its banks and the lives of fish and birds that depend on the river. The main problem is narrowing the rivers to shorten bridges. In addition, poorly planned bridges also damage navigable waterways.

Kanu Mia, a resident of Salehpur villageEver since the bridge was built, the river has become narrower. They have killed the river here with this bridge.

A Prothom Alo investigation has found that many bridges have been built without considering either the life of the river or navigability. Bridges are a source of distress not only for rivers but also for canals. Culverts, like bridges, can also be harmful. Yet no one keeps a complete record of such bridges and culverts, let alone takes steps to address the problem.

Responsibility for building these structures across rivers and canals repeatedly falls on the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED), the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, and the Roads and Highways Department (RHD). Political influence is also a factor.

Incomplete records

According to lists published on the websites of the National River Conservation Commission (NRCC) and the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) in 2025, Bangladesh has 1,415 rivers. However, no figure is available for the number of canals.

In December 2025, the BWDB compiled an incomplete list of infrastructure that obstructs the flow of rivers and canals, along with the agencies responsible for building them.

Prothom Alo obtained the list through an application under the Right to Information Act. It contains information on bridges, culverts, water-control structures such as regulators and sluice gates, embankments, roads and highways, as well as houses and shops.

The incomplete list shows that, among the harmful structures built on 52 rivers and 75 canals across 37 districts, bridges and culverts account for three-quarters of the total.

An executive engineer at the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) said structures that are generally four metres high and up to eight metres long are classified as culverts. Structures larger than that are considered bridges. Culverts are usually built over drains, he said.

According to the list, there are 193 harmful bridges and culverts on 30 rivers across 20 districts, with bridges accounting for the larger share. Meanwhile, 97 bridges and culverts have been built over 50 canals in 12 districts, with the two types of structures almost equal in number.

River flows decline during winter. Water resources experts say bridge designs have long been based on calculations of river flow during this season. As a result, water drainage is delayed during the monsoon, worsening flooding, said former Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) director general Md Enayet Ullah.

In addition, the NRCC has identified 57 such bridges on three other rivers. Prothom Alo reporters have continued to report on more such bridges at different times.

The BWDB list shows that the highest number of harmful bridges—48—are on the Bhairab River in Jashore and Jhenaidah. There are seven culverts too. The river is in a dying condition.

Prothom Alo’s Jashore correspondent has identified another bridge whose nameplate describes the Bhairab as a ‘canal’. The Kapotaksha River does not appear on the BWDB list. However, the correspondent has found 16 bridges over the river, all but one of which, were built in violation of regulations. These structures are choking the Kapotaksha.

The BWDB list shows that there are 17 harmful bridges on the Narad River in Natore and 16 on the Baral River in the same district. The Swai River, which flows through Mymensingh and Netrokona districts, has 14. On the Ayman River in Mymensingh, there are more culverts than bridges—15 in total. Harmful culverts are on all of these rivers.  

The list includes comments from the BWDB’s regional offices on the side of the names of 153 bridges or culverts. Nearly 90 per cent of the comments recommend increasing bridge lengths to match the widths of the rivers. They also recommend raising the bridges.

Low bridges are a major reason why a circular waterway around Dhaka could not become operational. Citing the Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA), a Prothom Alo report says there are 20 low bridges along the route, crossing the Buriganga, Turag, Tongi Canal (now recognised as a river), Balu, Shitalakkhya and Dhaleshwari rivers.

Of these, the BWDB list mentions only two bridges over the Tongi River. It does not include any other harmful bridges, including the Salehpur Bridge over the Turag. The NRCC, however, stated in its 2022 annual report that the bridge was shorter than the width of the river.

The same report highlighted how 22 bridges were narrowing the Balu River. At the Nila Market section of Purbachal New Town, it was found that the approach road to one of these bridges had been built inside the boundary marked by BIWTA’s boundary pillars.

The NRCC has also identified 14 harmful bridges on the Kaliganga River in Kushtia.

A bridge every few steps

A total of 21 bridges have been built along a 17-kilometre stretch of the Khakdon River in Barguna district. Meanwhile, three bridges stand within a distance of just 150 yards over the Tangon River in Thakurgaon town.

Most of the bridges over the Khakdon were built by the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED). Of the three over the Tangon, two were built by the Roads and Highways Department (RHD) and one by the LGED. Neither of these examples appears in the BWDB’s 2025 list of harmful infrastructure.

The River Conservation Commission provided Prothom Alo with the figures for the Khakdon. In its 2025 inspection report, the commission said that heavy and coarse silt accumulates in the Tangon and that regular dredging is essential. Erosion, pollution and encroachment are major problems affecting the river.

There is almost no water flow near the three bridges over the Tangon. The BWDB list identifies one vent pipe outlet—a water-control structure—as harmful infrastructure on the river.

Speaking about the Khakdon and Bhairab rivers, Sheikh Md Abu Zakir Sekandar, head of the LGED’s Bridge Design Section said, “The rivers in the areas you are referring to are not particularly wide, so these are certainly all small bridges. If the rivers were larger, so many bridges would not have been built.”

Meanwhile, a senior LGED official, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said the department had been forced to build bridges measuring 15, 20 and 30 metres under pressure from political leaders. When the pressure is intense, there is no way to refuse, the official said.

Another example of a poorly planned bridge was reported by Prothom Alo’s Kushtia correspondent. The Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief built it over the Kaliganga River in the Shalghar Madhua area of Kumarkhali upazila, Kushtia, around 12 years ago.

On paper, the river is 110 metres wide. However, it has narrowed as it has gradually filled up. Obstructing its flow, a dilapidated bridge measuring around 11 metres stands across the remaining stretch of water strewn with bushes and plants. There are no approach roads on either side, and the bridge is not in use.

A senior LGED official, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said the department had been forced to build bridges measuring 15, 20 and 30 metres under pressure from political leaders. When the pressure is intense, there is no way to refuse, the official said.

LGED tops the list

According to the BWDB list, the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED), an agency under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives, tops the list of builders of harmful structures on rivers and canals. The LGED has built 97 bridges and 24 culverts.

The Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief ranks second. The ministry, along with its relevant departments and upazila project implementation offices, is responsible for 45 bridges and 45 culverts. The third agency, the Roads and Highways Department (RHD), has built 24 bridges and three culverts.

The LGED has also built bridges jointly with other government agencies. These include 10 bridges built in partnership with the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, one with the RHD, and two with union parishads and upazila parishads. There are also some jointly built culverts. Local government bodies have also built several bridges and culverts independently.

Some of the bridges and culverts on the list were built by other government agencies, including Bangladesh Railway and the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC). Non-governmental organisations, businesspeople and entrepreneurs, individuals and local residents have also built one or two bridges or culverts each.

However, the BWDB list attributes only 12 harmful structures to the agency itself. Most of these are sluice gates or other water-control structures.

Irregularities begin with winter’s low water levels

River flows decline during winter. Water resources experts say bridge designs have long been based on calculations of river flow during this season. As a result, water drainage is delayed during the monsoon, worsening flooding, said former Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) director general Md Enayet Ullah.

Enayet Ullah was the BWDB director general when the list of harmful infrastructure was compiled. He told Prothom Alo, “The river is 500 feet wide, but a bridge was built with a span of just 300 feet. When we investigated why floodwaters took so long to recede during the 2024 floods in Feni, we found that the bridges in the area were a major problem.”

Ainun Nishat , waater resources expertWe have narrowed the rivers in this way. ... But why should those designs not be changed? Why should environmentally sound designs not be used?

Enayet Ullah said the bridges had been built without taking the rivers’ full width into account. A senior source at the National River Conservation Commission told Prothom Alo that the commission recommends building bridges based on the rivers’ cadastral survey (CS) maps. However, no agency has taken these recommendations into account over the past decade.

Water resources expert Ainun Nishat said that 50 years ago, small bridges and culverts were designed this way to reduce costs.

He told Prothom Alo, “We have narrowed the rivers in this way. ... But why should those designs not be changed? Why should environmentally sound designs not be used?”

Ainun Nishat primarily holds the LGED responsible. In his assessment, the Roads and Highways Department (RHD) ranks third on the list of responsible agencies. He also holds the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) and union parishad chairmen responsible. But who does he consider the second most responsible?

He said the problem was not limited to bridges and culverts only. Embankments, flood embankments or polders, and sluice gates also cause silt to accumulate, reducing rivers’ capacity to carry water. He therefore places the BWDB second, with poorly planned sluice gates holding the major share of responsibility.

When the BWDB compiled the list, Syeda Rizwana Hasan, chief executive of the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA), was the water resources adviser to the then interim government. She said most of the small bridges had been built long ago, when their impact on river flow was not taken into consideration.

Rizwana Hasan told Prothom Alo, however the bridge authorities, the Local Government Engineering Department, the Roads and Highways Department, the River Conservation Commission and the Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority share direct and equal responsibility when such small bridges are built today.

The Department of Environment would also be responsible if it approved such bridges, Rizwana Hasan said. She added that river width must be taken into account when bridges are built in future. Bridges that obstruct river flow must also be identified and modified.

Sheikh Md Abu Zakir Sekandar is the supervising engineer of the LGED’s Bridge Design Section. He said most of the narrow bridges are less than 100 metres long. The department’s project proposal guidelines stated that no surveys were required for these bridges, so none were carried out.

Accountability evaded amid irregularities

A reliable source of the Local Government Engineering Department’s (LGED) Bridge Design Section told Prothom Alo that the agency builds bridges based on the need for road connectivity at upazila, union and village levels. Besides, each political government has its own priorities for particular regions, where bridges and roads are built then.

The source said that, during feasibility assessments for bridges, clearance must be obtained from the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), the Department of Environment, the Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA) and, where applicable, the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (RAJUK).

In addition, if a bridge is 100 metres or longer, decisions must be made following surveys of water flow and the geographical characteristics of water bodies, known as hydromorphological surveys, along with other assessments.

Sheikh Md Abu Zakir Sekandar is the supervising engineer of the LGED’s Bridge Design Section. He said most of the narrow bridges are less than 100 metres long. The department’s project proposal guidelines stated that no surveys were required for these bridges, so none were carried out.

According to Abu Zakir, the problems arose because of the lack of surveys. However, he told Prothom Alo that, since 2005, they had also been conducting surveys for bridges shorter than 100 metres, taking into account their potentially harmful effects on river ecosystems.

An executive engineer of the Bridge Design Section, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said that in the 1960s and 1970s, bridges measuring 12 metres in length were built because of limited financial and technical capacity. More than two dozen such bridges were built over the Bhairab River up to the 1980s.

The LGED engineer said that, since 2003, the department had begun building bridges using standard designs that take river width into account. A guideline was also prepared in 2012, setting out detailed instructions on how to avoid harming rivers.

Md Enayet Ullah, the recently retired director general of the BWDB, also emphasised on the importance of surveys. He said that, in many cases, physical models should be prepared beforehand. However, circumstances may change later and create problems. There are also bridges with flawed designs, he added.

Enayet Ullah said there should be a legal requirement to seek the Water Development Board’s opinion before building bridges over rivers. The BWDB has no information on whether builders of the bridges are complying with rules.

An initial environmental assessment must be conducted before any bridge is built, and subsequent decisions are supposed to be based on its findings. However, a source at the Department of Environment’s clearance division told Prothom Alo that, in most cases, no assessment is carried out. The source however could not provide any specific figures.

Meanwhile, Sheikh Md Abu Zakir Sekandar of the LGED told Prothom Alo, “I admit that some low bridges have been built. However, if BIWTA had been active from the beginning, bridges of this kind would not have been built.”

Captain Md Shahjahan, director of BIWTA’s Navigation Conservation and Management Division, said the government first issued regulations in 2010 specifying how high bridges over different rivers should be. He said, “Before that, we had no role to play regarding bridge heights.”

The revised Rules for Construction of Structures in Inland Waterways, 2026, have now been introduced. Md Shahjahan said they are now determining bridge heights according to the classification of each river. However, some concessions are made for rivers that have lost their navigability.

A strong guardian needed

Different sides are making different statements, but the real loophole lies in the lack of care, responsibility, monitoring and accountability. There are plenty of laws, regulations and rules. But are they actually being followed? And who monitors compliance?

Following a High Court ruling, the government established the National River Conservation Commission in 2014 under an act. The commission works to ensure the flow of rivers, their ecological health and their use for multidimentional purposes, including as waterways.

On 28 May 2025, the River Commission held a workshop attended by officials from several public and private organisations, including the Bangladesh Water Development Board and the Local Government Engineering Department. The aim was to raise awareness about infrastructure that obstructs the flow of water in rivers, canals, wetlands and other water bodies.

Unplanned bridges killing rivers and waterways

Among the workshop’s recommendations was that low and short bridges should not be built, so that rivers remain navigable and water transport can move unobstructed. Bridges should span the full width of a river, from bank to bank. Also, multiple bridges should not be built in the same area unnecessarily.

The recommendations cover all types of infrastructure. They also address the need for relevant clearances, surveys and measures to remedy any damage. The interests of rivers must be given priority. Informing district river conservation committees and seeking the views of local people are also considered important.

The reccomendations also mentioned obtaining a no-objection certificate from the River Commission. Under the National River Protection Commission Act, the commission can only make recommendations. No one is legally obliged to follow the recommendations. Several commission members told Prothom Alo that no one pays heed to its recommendations.

Former chairman of the commission Mujibur Rahman Howlader told Prothom Alo that the government had no interest in enforcing the laws enacted to protect rivers or the rulings of the high courts. He said the government must take responsibility for the damage caused to rivers.

Mujibur Rahman Howlader said that saving rivers now required action from the Cabinet. District commissioners should be tasked with demarcating river boundaries and monitoring that they are not encroached upon. Those who violate the rules must face cases and punishment, he said.

Mujibur Rahman Howlader’s final point was that rivers would never be protected in the country without the government’s genuine willingness to do so.

Meanwhile, Sandhya Rani Sarkar, 57, who lives on the banks of Bhairab River, has a simple demand. The resident of Bagdanga village in Baghapara upazila of Jashore, told Prothom Alo’s Jashore correspondent, “I got married at the age of 25. Since then, I have bathed in the Bhairab and used its water.”

Sandhya Rani said the river has become somewhat wider and its current has increased slightly following recent dredging. However, she added, “The bridge on the river near our house is low and short. If the bridge were larger, the river would flow more freely.”

item.title: TOP SHOTS (17 November 2026)
Drugs once made abroad are now being produced in Bangladesh
item.description:
The Department of Narcotics Control (DNC) discovered a laboratory for processing ketamine, an anaesthetic drug, at a house in Uttara, Dhaka. Three Chinese nationals were arrested in a raid there on 25 March. According to officials, the group also received orders from abroad and sent drugs through courier services.

Uttara is not the only example. Recently, the DNC uncovered operations involving the production of new pills from crushed yaba tablets in Tongi, Gazipur; the cultivation of kush cannabis in Wari in Old Dhaka; and the production of adulterated alcohol in Bhatara, Dhaka. While new drugs continue to enter Bangladesh from abroad, cases of domestic production and processing are also coming to light.

The drug landscape is changing, as are the methods of buying and selling. Drugs are increasingly being found in e-cigarette (vape) liquids, on special paper and even in chocolates. Social media, private messaging groups and online shopping platforms are being used for distribution. Several raids have also revealed the involvement of young people and university students in this emerging drug market.

13 new drugs identified in 8 years

According to DNC data, at least 24 types of drugs are available in Bangladesh. Of these, 13 new or less commonly encountered substances were identified and seized between 2018 and 2025, an eight-year period. The highest number, five, were identified in 2019, while three were identified in 2021.

However, not all substances classified as new are entirely new chemicals; some are different forms of existing drugs.

The list includes khat (a stimulant plant), ice (crystalline methamphetamine, a powerful stimulant), MDMA or ecstasy (a synthetic stimulant), LSD (a hallucinogenic chemical), tapentadol and tramadol (opioid painkillers), DMT (a hallucinogenic chemical), magic mushrooms (fungi containing psychoactive substances), DOB (a synthetic hallucinogen), kush (a potent variety of cannabis), high-purity heroin (an opiate), black cocaine (a particular form of cocaine) and MDMB (a synthetic chemical that produces effects similar to cannabis).

Some of these substances are stimulants, while others cause hallucinations. Certain substances are also used as medicines. Tapentadol and tramadol, for example, are painkillers.

DNC officials say MDMA is primarily used at clubs and parties. There is evidence that it is being brought into Bangladesh from the United Kingdom and the Netherlands. In September 2025, a total of 317 tablets were seized from a consignment sent by post from the UK.

MDMB found in vape liquid

The DNC says MDMB was most recently identified as a new drug in December 2025. The substance, brought from Malaysia, was being supplied for use through e-cigarettes, or vapes, which heat liquid into vapour for inhalation.

Acting on intelligence, the DNC seized 340 millilitres of the liquid and arrested four members of the network. According to the agency, three of them were university students and the fourth was an employee of a private company.

Citing information obtained during the investigation, the DNC said one member of the group regularly travelled to Malaysia to collect the drug. The target market was affluent and upper-middle-class consumers in Dhaka.

To sell the substance, the group posted coded messages in private Facebook groups and through fake accounts. Interested buyers were subsequently contacted on WhatsApp to negotiate prices and arrange delivery. Group members used emojis as coded signals to communicate locations.

Although MDMA and MDMB have similar names, they are two different drugs. The former is a stimulant, while the latter belongs to a class of synthetic chemicals that produce effects similar to cannabis.

DNC officials say even a small quantity of MDMB can have serious effects on the nervous system. It carries risks of hallucinations and abnormal heart rhythms. Its liquid form also makes it easy to transport and difficult to detect.

Production and processing in residential buildings

DNC officials say several networks involved in producing drugs in residential buildings have been identified in Dhaka and surrounding areas this year.

The three Chinese nationals arrested at the ketamine-processing laboratory in Uttara are accused of taking orders through the dark web and sending drugs by courier. Their reported destinations included Malaysia, Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, and Sri Lanka. Transactions were conducted in cryptocurrency, a form of digital currency.

On 19 February, the DNC announced that it had uncovered a drug-processing facility in a house in Tongi. According to officials, around 500 yaba tablets were crushed and mixed with colouring agents and chemicals to produce approximately 5,000 new tablets.

Rather than producing the original chemical substance, this operation involved processing an existing drug into a different form.

On 7 January, the DNC also uncovered kush cultivation in a temperature-controlled room in Wari. In a separate raid, equipment used to produce adulterated alcohol was found in a flat in Bhatara.

In August 2022, the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) announced the first seizure of kush in Bangladesh after recovering the substance in Gulshan. The person arrested in that case was accused of cultivating kush under controlled conditions in Mohammadpur. Investigators also found information indicating that seeds had been brought from the United States and the Netherlands.

Drugs found in paper, liquid and chocolate

The emergence of new forms of drugs is making detection increasingly challenging. According to the DNC, besides cannabis sold in small packets and yaba tablets, authorities are finding crystalline ice, LSD-soaked blotter paper (small pieces of paper infused with chemicals), vape liquids and chocolates containing drugs.

In 2022, kush, LSD, cocaine, ecstasy and chocolates containing cannabis-derived substances were seized from a flat in Banani. There were also seizures of vape liquids and drug-laced chocolates in 2025.

Abdul Halim Raj, an assistant director of the DNC, told Prothom Alo that new packaging and methods of consumption were making it difficult to identify these substances from their appearance alone. However, not all cases involve the creation of new chemicals; in some instances, existing drugs are simply being transported or consumed in different forms.

Online orders, home delivery

The use of technology in the drug trade is increasing.

After recovering 300 grams of cannabis in Bhatara on 16 October, the DNC uncovered an online network centred around university students. The agency said kush and synthetic cannabis were being sold through websites and private Telegram groups linked to two private universities in Bashundhara.

The group had around 250 student members. Cards containing QR codes were distributed to facilitate access to the group. Drugs were ordered online and delivered to buyers' homes.

On 16 August, the DNC arrested Anisur Rahman from Satarkul in Badda with 620 millilitres of liquid THC. Investigators said he had been selling the drug through courier services under the label of CBD oil. They found evidence that he had sold around 405 bottles over five years.

Earlier, on 5 July 2025, the DNC seized 138 pieces of LSD-infused blotter paper during raids in Bhatara and Bashundhara. According to the agency, a forensic examination of the equipment belonging to the person arrested in the case revealed evidence of drug purchases through the dark web and payments in Bitcoin.

In November 2021, 90 pieces of blotter paper containing DOB were recovered from two young men in Khulna. The DNC said they had arranged to bring the substance from Poland through the dark web.

People and organisations working on drug-related issues say curiosity about new substances among regular drug users is creating a market for emerging drugs. Young people make up a large proportion of consumers.

A study by Bangladesh Medical University found that 33 per cent of drug users had first taken drugs between the ages of 8 and 17. Another 59 per cent started between the ages of 18 and 25. This means 92 per cent began using drugs by the age of 25.

Mohammad Mehedi Hasan, deputy director of the DNC's Dhaka Divisional Intelligence Office, told Prothom Alo that a large proportion of buyers of new synthetic drugs came from affluent and educated backgrounds.

Drug traders were exploiting their access to technology to sell substances discreetly, he said.

Uncertainty over 'zombie drugs'

A video showing a young man behaving unusually on a footpath in Shahbagh recently went viral on social media. The caption described him as being under the influence of a 'zombie drug'.

Several DNC officials said that after reviewing the video and making inquiries about the young man, they were reasonably certain that drugs were involved. However, the DNC has yet to seize any such substance in Bangladesh.

Officials explain that 'zombie' is not the chemical name of a particular drug. Abroad, substances marketed or described as zombie drugs have been found to contain a combination of fentanyl, an extremely potent synthetic opioid, and xylazine, a sedative used in veterinary medicine.

Their effects can include extreme drowsiness and impaired movement. Such combinations are commonly referred to as 'zombie drugs' in other countries.

DNC officials say they have found evidence of fentanyl in Bangladesh's drug market, but have not yet identified xylazine.

Challenges in detecting new drugs

There are significant gaps in the technological capacity needed to identify and control emerging drugs. DNC officials say many members of other law enforcement agencies are unable to detect all types of synthetic drugs. As a result, some consignments may escape detection.

Preparations are under way to install drug-detection equipment at airports. Meanwhile, controlling domestic drug production and online sales through digital platforms and private groups has created additional challenges.

Mohammad Hasan Maruf, director general of the Department of Narcotics Control, told Prothom Alo that demand for new drugs was growing among young people, while an increasing variety of substances was entering the country from abroad.

The DNC is working to identify and control these drugs with a workforce of just 3,000, he said. The agency has already seized kush, MDMB and ketamine, identified domestic laboratories and taken action against those involved.

However, despite reports of seizures of emerging drugs, the full picture of their market and spread remains unclear. This raises a crucial question: while isolated raids have led to the seizure of small quantities of new drugs, how much progress has actually been made in identifying the networks operating behind the trade?

item.title: Workers halt operations at 2 Chittagong port terminals, stage protest
item.description:
Workers have suspended the loading and unloading of containers from ships at the two main terminals of Chittagong Port. 

They halted operations at both terminals from the first shift at 8:00 am today, Tuesday, demanding payment of financial benefits, including gratuity.

The two terminals are the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and the Chittagong Container Terminal (CCT). 

58 per cent of the port’s total container handling took place at these two terminals last fiscal year.

According to port sources, although the Bangladesh Navy-owned Chittagong Dry Dock Limited is officially responsible for operating the NCT, Saif Powertec Limited is carrying out its actual operational activities. Saif Powertec also operates the CCT.

The government has signed an agreement to hand over the operation of the NCT to Dubai-based port operator DP World. The terminal is expected to be handed over to the company within the next few months. Meanwhile, steps are also under way to transfer the operation of the CCT from Saif Powertec to a foreign operator.

Against this backdrop, the jobs of around 1,000 regular workers and employees at the two terminals have come under uncertainty.

A worker said those employed at the two terminals had been demanding payment of various financial benefits, including gratuity, accrued leave and incentives. As they did not receive these benefits, they stopped work at both terminals this morning.

The workers’ programme has halted container loading and unloading operations involving six ships at the terminals. Terminal operations have also come to a standstill.

When contacted for comment, Saif Powertec Limited Managing Director Tarfadar Ruhul Amin did not answer his mobile phone. Chattogram Port Secretary Syed Refayet Hamim also did not respond to calls.

Asked about the situation, a port official told Prothom Alo that discussions with the workers were under way and operations were expected to resume soon.

item.title: Pori Moni’s drug case: Indictment hearing scheduled for today
item.description:
A hearing on the framing of charges against film actress Pori Moni and two others in a case filed under the Narcotics Control Act at Banani police station in the capital is scheduled to be held today, Tuesday.

The hearing will take place at Dhaka Special Judge Court-10. Pori Moni’s lawyer, Nilanjana Rifat Surabhi, confirmed the matter to Prothom Alo.

She said the hearing on charge framing would be held today in Pori Moni’s presence.

Pori Moni goes live on Facebook at midnight, alleges attack on her car

The hearing had previously been scheduled for 29 September. However, Pori Moni could not appear in court that day because of "pain in the legs". Following an appeal by her lawyer, the court later postponed the hearing and fixed 17 November as the new date.

On 4 August 2021, the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) raided Pori Moni’s home in Banani, in the capital. RAB claimed at the time that a large quantity of foreign liquor and other narcotics had been seized from her home.

‘How dare he touch me!’ Enraged Pori Moni at court premises

Pori Moni was arrested in connection with a case filed by RAB at Banani police station over the incident. She was later released on bail.

On 5 January 2022, the trial court ordered the framing of charges against Pori Moni and two others in the case. The other two accused are her manager, Ashraful Islam Dipu, and her maternal uncle, Kabir Hossain Howlader.

After the charges were framed, Pori Moni filed an appeal with the High Court seeking the cancellation of the case. The High Court disposed of the appeal in a ruling with observations. An order was subsequently issued for charges to be framed again in the case.

item.title: HC upholds Sohel Rana’s death sentence in Pallabi child rape, murder case
item.description:
The High Court has upheld the death sentence of Sohel Rana, one of two convicts sentenced to death by a trial court for the rape and murder of a seven-year-old girl in Pallabi, Mirpur, in the capital.
The verdict was delivered by a High Court bench comprising Justice Bhishmadev Chakrabortty and Justice KM Rasheduzzaman Raja. Proceedings began at 10:38am on Tuesday. The date for the verdict was set after hearings on the appeals and death references concluded on Monday.
According to case documents, the victim's father, who works at a private office in Banani, lived with his family in a rented flat in Pallabi. Sohel Rana and Swapna Khatun lived in another flat in the same building. The child was a second-grade student.
The child was raped and murdered on May 19. After the crime, Sohel Rana fled by cutting through the window grille of the room. Acting on information received through the national emergency service 999, police took Swapna Khatun into custody, while Sohel Rana was arrested near Fatullah Police Station in Narayanganj.
The victim's father filed a case at Pallabi Police Station. On May 21, Sohel Rana gave a confessional statement before a court under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Both accused were subsequently sent to prison.
On May 25, the investigating officer, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station, submitted a charge sheet against Sohel Rana and his wife, Swapna Khatun. The case was also referred to the tribunal for trial that day.
The trial formally began on June 1, when charges were framed against the two accused. The following day, 16 prosecution witnesses testified, completing the recording of witness statements in a single day. On June 3, the accused were examined under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
On June 7, Judge Masrur Salekin of the Dhaka Metropolitan Tribunal for the Prevention of Violence Against Children delivered the verdict.
The tribunal ordered that both accused be hanged by the neck until dead under Section 368 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Under Section 374, the death sentences were referred to the High Court Division for confirmation.
The tribunal also fined Sohel Rana Tk5 lakh and Swapna Khatun Tk2 lakh, ordering that the money be paid to the victim's legal heirs.
It further ordered that if the fines remained unpaid, the Collectorate office could attach and sell the accused's movable and immovable properties, with the proceeds going to the victim's legal heirs.
The verdict was delivered just 19 days after the murder.
Following the trial court's judgment, the death reference, containing the relevant case documents, was sent to the High Court. Both accused subsequently filed jail appeals.

item.title: Postponed RMG wage board meeting rescheduled for Nov 23
item.description:
The postponed third meeting of the Minimum Wage Board, formed to set a new wage structure for garment workers, will be held on November 23.
At the meeting, the owners' representatives will present their proposed minimum wage, according to a board notice issued on Tuesday.
The third meeting was originally scheduled for Monday, when the owners' side was expected to present its wage proposal. They were also prepared for the meeting. However, it was postponed at the last minute, citing unavoidable circumstances.
It was later learnt that the meeting was postponed because workers' representative Md Anwar Hossain had fallen ill.
At the board's second meeting on November 9, the workers' representatives submitted their wage proposal, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk32,000 for garment workers.
The owners' side, however, did not submit any proposal at the meeting and sought seven working days to prepare one. The board instead gave them four working days to submit their proposal.
Worker unrest has continued across the garment sector for the past two weeks over demands for higher wages. Workers at various factories have been leaving workplaces without working after marking their attendance. Protests and clashes with law enforcers have also been reported in several areas.
Amid the situation, the government formed the Minimum Wage Board on November 1 to revise garment workers' wages. The board held its first meeting on November 4, where it agreed to implement the new wage structure from next month.
However, despite ongoing discussions over workers' demands, unrest in the industrial zones has not completely subsided.
The unrest has disrupted production and export activities at garment factories. To manage the situation, many factory owners have been forced to shut down their facilities under Section 13(1) of the Labour Act, 2006.
A total of 104 factories were closed under this provision on Sunday, while the number rose to 132 on Monday.

item.title: Garment workers block roads as unrest returns to Savar, Ashulia
item.description:
The industrial zones in Savar and Ashulia turned tense again on Tuesday after remaining calm for two days, as workers staged protests, clashed with police and blocked roads at several locations over their demand for higher minimum wages.
Police fired tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse the protesters, disrupting traffic on the Dhaka-Aricha Highway and causing long tailbacks.
Around 9:30am, workers of Standard Group gathered on the road near Padma Mor in Hemayetpur, under Tetuljhora union in Savar, instead of entering their factory. They later attempted to block the road by dumping waste and setting it on fire.
When police and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) members tried to clear the road, clashes broke out between the two sides. Workers threw bricks and stones at police, prompting law enforcers to fire tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse them.
The workers later scattered and took positions on different roads and in nearby alleys. Intermittent clashes continued in the area.
Meanwhile, workers entered several nearby factories but reportedly continued work stoppages inside.
In another incident, workers attempted to block roads in the Khejurbagan area of Ashulia after 8:30am. Police fired tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse them.
Around 11am, workers from several garment factories blocked the Dhaka-Aricha Highway in Rajfulbaria, Savar, bringing traffic to a standstill.
Sub-Inspector Ibn-e-Farhad of Savar Model Police Station said workers from several factories, had gathered on the highway. Police and BGB members were working to restore normal traffic, he added.
Ali Ahmed, officer-in-charge of Savar Highway Police Station, said workers blocked the Dhaka-Aricha Highway in the Fulbaria area around 11am.
Asaduzzaman Noor, in-charge of Savar Highway Police Station, said traffic remained suspended as workers occupied the highway, causing long tailbacks on both sides. Police were working to restore normal traffic, he added.
Workers continued their blockade until 11:50am.
Eight factories in the industrial zone remained closed on Tuesday under Section 13(1) of the Labour Act, 2006.
Three others announced general holidays, while workers at five factories were observing work stoppages.
Savar Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Md Saiful Islam said law enforcers dispersed workers who attempted to block roads in Ashulia.
He added that workers also tried to block the Hemayetpur-Keraniganj Road, prompting law enforcers to fire tear gas shells and sound grenades to clear the road.
A total of 18 platoons of BGB have been deployed alongside police to maintain order in Savar and Ashulia, he said.
At around 11:15am, Savar Highway Police Station Officer-in-Charge Ali Ahmed said protesters were still blocking the road. Dhaka district police, Industrial Police and highway police were jointly working to clear the road, and he expressed hope that the situation would be resolved soon.

item.title: Two crude bombs explode near Dhaka airport, three injured
item.description:
Two crude bombs exploded near the outer gate of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and in Uttara’s Jasimuddin area on Monday night, injuring three pedestrians.
Kamrul Islam Talukdar, officer-in-charge of Airport Police Station, said miscreants detonated the two bombs, leaving three pedestrians with minor injuries.
He added that the bombs were thrown from a flyover and security measures had since been strengthened.

item.title: 42 BGB platoons deployed in Dhaka, Gazipur, Narayanganj
item.description:
A total of 42 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed in industrial areas across Dhaka, Gazipur and Narayanganj to maintain law and order and ensure public safety, according to BGB headquarters.
Of the deployed personnel, 20 platoons are in Dhaka, covering Mirpur, Savar, Hemayetpur and Ashulia, including areas near Yunus Convention Hall, Kathgara, Zirabo, Hameem Group, Midlar Group and Jamgara.
Another 15 platoons have been deployed in Gazipur, covering Chandra, Palli Bidyut, Mouchak, Konabari, Telirchala, Kashimpur, Bhogra Bypass, Gacha, Sataish and Salna.
The remaining seven platoons are stationed in Narayanganj, covering Shibu Market, Katherpul, Jalkuri, the BSCIC Industrial Estate, Chashara Mor, Kanchpur Bridge and Shimrail.
BGB headquarters is conducting continuous, technology-driven surveillance to monitor developments on the ground and coordinate operations, the force said.
The monitoring includes real-time footage from drones, body-worn cameras and other specialised equipment.
The BGB said it remains on high alert in coordination with the local administration and police to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and respond to any untoward incidents in the industrial zones.
The force added that it is maintaining constant surveillance and taking necessary measures as the situation evolves.

item.title: Minimum wage protest halts traffic in Mirpur
item.description:
Garment workers blocked roads in the capital's Mirpur area on Tuesday, demanding an increase in the minimum monthly wage to Tk30,000.
The blockade has halted traffic in both directions between Mirpur-10 and Mirpur-12.
Around 8:30am on Tuesday, several factories announced closures, prompting most workers to return home.
However, workers from several garment factories staged protests and blocked the road beneath the Pallabi-11 metro rail station.
The protesters were chanting various slogans.
Additional police personnel and members of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) were deployed at the scene to maintain order.
Pallabi police station Officer-in-Charge Md Jalal Uddin said efforts were underway to remove the workers from the road.
He added that police were on alert to prevent any untoward situation.

item.title: 10 platoons BGB deployed in Gopalganj
item.description:
Ten platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel have been deployed in key areas of Gopalganj to maintain law and order and ensure public security.
The deployed personnel are carrying out their duties in coordination with the local administration and police.
The BGB Media Department disclosed the information on Tuesday.
According to the BGB, its headquarters' monitoring cell is maintaining technology-based surveillance to closely monitor the law and order situation and coordinate field operations.
Live footage from drones, body-worn cameras and improvised devices is being monitored round the clock.

item.title: Crude bomb explodes at Mirpur Model Police Station
item.description:
A crude bomb exploded at Mirpur Model Police Station in the capital around 11am on Tuesday. No casualties or property damage have been reported.
Mizanur Rahman, a police officer on duty at the station, said: “We are inside the police station. Our personnel are stationed out front; they would be able to provide more information.”
However, Officer-in-Charge Hafizur Rahman said sound grenades had been deployed in response to a protest by garment workers, adding that the loud noise heard in the area was caused by the detonation of the grenades.
Multiple sources, however, confirmed that a cocktail had exploded at the police station.

item.title: Police, BGB fire tear gas, sound grenades as Gazipur workers block roads
item.description:
Workers from several factories staged protests in Gazipur's Joydebpur and Chandana Chowrasta areas on Tuesday, demanding an increase in the minimum wage.
Their road blockades since the morning disrupted traffic on the Dhaka-Mymensingh Highway, Joydebpur Road and Bhogra Bypass.
Police and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) members fired tear gas shells and sound grenades to bring the situation under control, triggering chases and counter-chases between workers and law enforcers
However, the workers refused to leave the roads despite the measures.
Workers also attempted to block the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in the Naojor area over the same demand. Law enforcers later removed them from the road.
According to police and local sources, workers from several factories in Joydebpur and Chandana Chowrasta began protesting around 9am without joining their shifts. Hundreds of workers from different factories later gathered and took positions on the roads.
At one stage, they blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh Highway and Joydebpur Road, bringing traffic to a standstill.
Police and BGB members went to the scene and asked the workers to clear the roads. The situation soon escalated, leading to chases and counter-chases between the two sides.
Law enforcers later fired tear gas shells and sound grenades in an attempt to disperse the workers, but they continued their blockade.
Mohammad Amzad Hossain, superintendent of police of Gazipur Industrial Zone-2, said workers from several nearby factories had blocked the roads.
Law enforcers were working to remove them and restore normal traffic, he added.

item.title: Former DSCC mayor Sayeed Khokon arrested in Dhaka
item.description:
Former Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) mayor Mohammad Sayeed Khokon has been arrested from a residence in the capital's Baridhara area.
He was arrested around 7am on Tuesday.
According to a statement from the Special Response Battalion (SRB), a team of SRB-01 arrested him from House 13 on Road 9 in Baridhara.
Following his arrest, Sayeed Khokon was placed in the custody of Gulshan police station.
Further legal proceedings against him are underway, the statement said.

item.title: Nahid condemns attack on expatriate Bangladeshis, students in London
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) Convener and opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam has accused activists of the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned, of attacking expatriate Bangladeshis and students from various universities after a reception held in London, saying several people were injured.
In a Facebook post on Tuesday, Nahid blamed what he described as “fugitive and extremist activists of the Awami League” for the attack and strongly condemned the incident.
In his post, Nahid said expatriate Bangladeshis from different parts of the UK, students from various universities, community leaders and leaders of the 11-party alliance attended the reception in London. He expressed deep gratitude and appreciation for their large turnout.
He alleged that after the event, fugitive activists of the Awami League attacked ordinary expatriate Bangladeshis and university students who had attended the program, leaving several people injured. He also wished the injured a speedy recovery.
Nahid said representatives of international human rights organisations and journalists from various media outlets were present at the event and witnessed the attack and violence firsthand. He expressed hope that the incident would draw international attention based on their firsthand accounts and collected information.
In his Facebook post, he said the people of Bangladesh had witnessed the Awami League's history of political violence, repression and destruction of democratic institutions.
He said individuals linked to the political force, which was ousted from power through the July uprising, were now attempting to suppress dissent through violence and intimidation even on foreign soil.
Such actions, he said, raised concerns not only about the safety of expatriate Bangladeshis but also about the democratic environment and political freedom.
“There is no right to use the opportunities of democracy to perpetrate anti-democratic violence,” he said.
Nahid added that using political asylum, freedom of expression and the right to assembly in a democratic country like the UK as tools for violence and intimidation was unacceptable.
He called on the UK government to ensure a prompt, impartial and effective investigation into the incident.
He also demanded legal action against those involved in the attack and effective measures to prevent acts of terrorism and violence carried out under the cover of the UK's democratic space.

item.title: Awami League, NCP activists clash in London, four injured
item.description:
At least four people were injured in clashes between activists of the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned and the National Citizen Party (NCP) on a road behind London's Mayfair Hall following a reception for NCP Convener and opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam on Monday night.
The injured were admitted to local hospitals, while London police baton-charged protesters several times to bring the situation under control.
Members of the British-Bangladeshi community and prominent figures expressed strong dismay over the incident, saying that bringing political rivalries from Bangladesh to London was deeply embarrassing for the entire community.
The reception was organised at Mayfair Hall in central London by members of the British-Bangladeshi community as part of Nahid Islam's week-long visit to the UK.
During the event, activists of the Awami League and its affiliated organisations gathered outside the venue.
According to eyewitnesses and organisers, Awami League supporters threw eggs and water bottles at guests arriving at the event and confronted them outside the hall.
After the program ended, activists of the Awami League and the NCP engaged in chasing and counter-chasing, followed by around 20 minutes of scuffles on the road behind the hall.
Saiful Islam, Prothom Alo's UK correspondent who was present at the venue, said Nahid Islam entered Mayfair Hall at around 3pm, more than three hours ahead of the scheduled time. He was therefore able to enter before the protesters gathered.
Nahid avoided any direct confrontation as he left the venue through a back entrance instead of the main gate after the event.
The incident sparked strong reactions among British-Bangladeshi residents, civil society representatives and guests attending the programme.
Cultural organiser Mahbubur Rahman Shiblu said the long-standing culture of such disruptive behaviour must end so that community events abroad are not overshadowed by street violence.

item.title: Titumir: Every taka borrowed must deliver maximum economic, social benefits
item.description:
Prime Minister's Adviser on Finance and Planning Dr Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir today said the government is focusing not on how much it borrows, but on ensuring that every unit of public resources generates the maximum possible economic and social benefits.
"We are not debating whether we should borrow less or borrow more. Rather, our focus is on how to borrow better, invest better and ensure the highest economic and social returns from every unit of public resources, while remaining accountable to the people," he said.
He was speaking as the chief guest at the concluding session of the two-day 'International Debt Conference Bangladesh 2026' in Cox's Bazar.
Describing borrowing as a means rather than an end to development, Dr Titumir said borrowed funds should be invested in sectors that enhance productivity, improve infrastructure, create employment opportunities and develop human resources.
He stressed that the economic and social returns from borrowing must be commensurate with the liabilities passed on to future generations.
Highlighting the challenging economic circumstances facing Bangladesh, the adviser said geopolitical conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East had increased the country's energy import expenditure by $4.2 billion.
"This additional expenditure was neither our choice nor something we could avoid," he said.
Referring to the human impact of the economic pressures, he said around eight million Bangladeshis had fallen below the poverty line again amid inflation and economic disruptions.
Many people who had worked hard to escape poverty were pushed back into it, he said, adding that these were not merely figures in statistical records but real hardships affecting people's lives.
Dr Titumir said the figures were not intended to blame anyone but to explain the circumstances in which the present government began its journey.
Understanding the starting point, he added, was essential to properly assess progress and the challenges ahead.
Describing the country's debt situation, he said Bangladesh's public debt had exceeded Tk18.9 trillion, equivalent to around 36% of GDP. Total external debt of the public and private sectors stood at more than $104 billion.
The government was spending over Tk1 trillion annually on interest payments alone. In addition, he said, Tk 56,750 crore had previously been borrowed from Bangladesh Bank to finance the budget deficit.
Emphasising the need for prudent debt management, he said the government must take all existing liabilities and associated risks into account while formulating its borrowing strategy.
As grace periods on previously contracted external loans were coming to an end, debt repayment pressures would increase in the coming years, he noted.
Bangladesh repaid $4.49 billion in principal and interest on external loans in the fiscal year 2025-26, and the annual repayment amount could rise to $7.6 billion by FY2030, he said.
Therefore, he stressed, decisions on new borrowing must carefully consider interest rates, maturity periods, repayment schedules, currency composition and exchange-rate risks.
Identifying national ownership and credibility as two fundamental pillars of debt management, Dr Titumir said borrowing decisions must be aligned with the country's development priorities and economic realities.
Transparency regarding debt data, expenditure and risks, alongside accountability to the public, was directly linked to the credibility of government debt management, he added.
The adviser also identified increased revenue mobilisation as a key condition for sustainable debt management.
Noting that Bangladesh's tax-to-GDP ratio remained low, he said the government aimed to increase the revenue-to-GDP ratio by two percentage points over the next five years.
The target would be pursued through expanding the tax base, digitalising tax administration and bringing more economic activities into the formal sector, he said. Higher revenue collection would help maintain a balance between development expenditure and debt servicing.
Highlighting the government's initiatives, Dr Titumir said the present government had stopped borrowing from Bangladesh Bank to finance the budget deficit.
As a result, pressure on money supply had eased and inflation had started declining from around 10%. Foreign exchange reserves had also risen above $30 billion, he said.
He further said the interest rate on 91-day Treasury bills had declined from around 12% to nearly 8%. The government had also taken initiatives to mobilise financing through long-term bonds and Sukuk.
Emphasising the need to develop the domestic capital market as a source of long-term financing, he said Bangladesh must maintain a balanced mix of domestic and external borrowing, short-term and long-term financing, and concessional and market-based loans.
He also stressed the importance of exploring alternative financing mechanisms, including private investment, public-private partnerships (PPPs), blended finance and credit guarantees.
Regarding the use of new financial instruments, including sovereign Sukuk, the adviser said Bangladesh's local-currency government securities had been included in JP Morgan's GBI-EM index.
He described the inclusion as an important milestone for the country's domestic currency bond market.
Alongside strengthening the capacity of the domestic bond market for long-term financing, Bangladesh also had opportunities to raise funds from international capital markets in a responsible and sustainable manner, he added.
Dr Titumir underscored the need for institutional reforms in debt management, including the establishment of a dedicated debt management office, enactment of a Public Debt Act and strengthening analytical capacity for debt data and risk assessment.
Regular publication of debt information, a medium-term debt strategy, an annual borrowing plan and transparent disclosure of contingent liabilities arising from government guarantees would help identify fiscal risks in advance, he said.
Outlining the government's strategy for economic transformation, he identified three phases:
He said the country aimed to move forward through economic recovery, restoration of institutional capacity and structural reconstruction.
Referring to Bangladesh's aspiration to become a US$1 trillion economy by 2034, he identified production, industrialisation, export capacity and employment generation as the key drivers of economic transformation.
Highlighting the economic importance of social protection programmes, the adviser said initiatives such as the Family Card and Farmer Card would contribute to improving living standards, reducing poverty and expanding economic inclusion.
These programmes were not merely forms of assistance but strategic investments in human development and long-term economic capacity, he said.
He also noted that the World Bank and development partners viewed these initiatives as part of the government's planned and financially responsible strategy.
Dr Titumir said the success of debt management should not be measured merely by how much money a country borrowed or repaid.
Rather, the real measure of success would be the extent to which borrowed funds transformed the economy and people's lives and generated economic and social benefits for future generations, he added.
The two-day conference, held on November 15-16, discussed sustainable sovereign debt management, borrowing costs and risks, international bond markets, the IMF's debt sustainability assessment framework, development of domestic bond markets and alternative sources of financing.
Around 100 delegates from nearly 30 countries, including Bangladesh, participated in the conference jointly organised by the Finance Division and the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
Participants included officials from the Finance Ministry and Bangladesh Bank, debt management experts from different countries, and representatives of the World Bank, IMF and ADB.
Representatives from the debt management offices of Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Indonesia and Malaysia also attended the conference.

item.title: National University VC freed after 12-hour standoff; offices closed for three days
item.description:
National University Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr ASM Amanullah was freed after being confined to his office for around 12 hours amid a protest by 988 reinstated staff members over their demands.
He was able to leave his office at around 11:30pm on Monday after the staff members staged a day-long siege and sit-in, pressing for resolution of issues related to seniority, promotions and outstanding salaries and allowances.
Meanwhile, the university authorities have decided to keep all university offices closed for three days, from Tuesday to Thursday, to address the situation.
The decision was taken at an emergency meeting of the university’s Syndicate on Monday night. It was announced in a press release signed by Taiyeba Tasneem Siraj, acting director of the National University’s Public Relations Department.
According to the release, all university offices will remain closed from November 17 to 19. However, essential services, the Office of the Controller of Examinations and activities related to the Principals' Conference will remain operational.
The 988 reinstated staff members had been protesting for the second consecutive day, demanding resolution of issues including seniority, promotions and payment of outstanding salaries and allowances.
They began surrounding the vice-chancellor’s office at the university’s main campus in Gazipur on Monday morning. At one point, they locked the main gate, effectively bringing the campus to a standstill and preventing the vice-chancellor from leaving his office.
The protesters said they had been reinstated following a court order but had continued to face discrimination over seniority, promotions and salary and allowance payments. They also alleged that they were being denied the benefits of the current pay scale.
They further claimed that while the university continued to recruit new staff and spend money in other areas, no effective steps had been taken to settle their outstanding dues.
On Sunday, the staff members had also surrounded the vice-chancellor’s office to submit a memorandum outlining their demands.
Amid the impasse, an emergency Syndicate meeting was convened at 10pm on Monday at the vice-chancellor’s office on the university’s main campus. The meeting was chaired by Professor Amanullah, and the decision to close university offices for three days was taken there.
In a Facebook post around 8pm on Monday, the vice-chancellor alleged that the 988 reinstated officers and employees had confined him for nine hours.
“My administration will not take any action that goes against the interests of the National University. I have acted in accordance with the court's verdict; for the rest, I will follow the government's directives. I have never bowed to pressure in the past, and I will not do so now,” he wrote.
He also said the university needed reform and that he had taken several initiatives towards that goal, but such efforts could not succeed if he was prevented from working.
Describing the blockade and confinement as futile, he wrote: “You have held me confined for nine hours; even if you were to keep me confined for 90 hours, it would achieve nothing.”
The officers and employees concerned were appointed to various positions between November 17, 2003, and August 31, 2004, but were dismissed from service in 2012, leading to a prolonged legal battle.
On May 27, 2025, a seven-member bench of the Appellate Division ordered the reinstatement of the surviving dismissed staff members. The court directed that their period of dismissal be treated as “extraordinary leave” and that their seniority be preserved.
However, the university authorities were tasked with determining matters relating to salaries, allowances and other benefits, taking humanitarian and practical considerations into account.
Following the implementation of the court verdict, the 988 reinstated staff members began protesting for recognition of their seniority, promotions and payment of outstanding salaries and allowances. The latest demonstration brought normal activities on the university’s main campus to a halt, prompting the authorities to call an emergency Syndicate meeting and announce the three-day office closure.

item.title: Bangladesh face Macau in AFC U-17 Asian Cup qualifiers today
item.description:
Bangladesh U-17 national football team face Macau in their crucial third group match of the 2027 AFC U-17 Asian Cup qualification scheduled to be held on Tuesday at Saud Bin Saqr Al Qasimi Stadium in Ras Al Khaimah, the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
The match kicks off at 5.20 pm [Bangladesh time].
Earlier, Bangladesh began their campaign with a 5-1 goals defeat to Syria in their opening group stage match but staged a brilliant fight back to register a convincing 4-0 victory over Bhutan in their second group match. Bangladesh pitted in group C along with Syria, Bhutan, Macau and the UAE, will play their ultimate group match against the host UAE on November 20. The champion team of the group will qualify in the final round.

item.title: Holders India, first-time finalists Pakistan face off in SAFF final
item.description:
Defending champions India will take on first-time finalists Pakistan in the SAFF Championship 2026 final at the National Stadium in Dhaka on Tuesday.
India are aiming to secure a record-extending 10th title and become the first team to win three consecutive editions of the regional competition. Pakistan, meanwhile, will be looking to lift their maiden SAFF Championship trophy in their first-ever final appearance.
Scheduled to kick off at 8pm, the final promises to be a fascinating contest between the traditional rivals, with India seeking to extend their dominance and Pakistan hoping to script a historic triumph.
India are the most successful team in SAFF Championship history, having lifted the trophy in 1993, 1997, 1999, 2005, 2009, 2011, 2015, 2021 and 2023.
Despite their dominance, India have never won the championship in three consecutive editions. A victory on Tuesday would see them achieve that milestone while further extending their record.
Head coach Naushad Moosa's young side booked their place in the final with a 2-1 victory over Bhutan in the first semifinal. PV Vishnu and captain Chinglensana Singh Konsham scored in the first half to give India a two-goal cushion before Kinzang Tashi Tobden pulled one back shortly after the break.
Pakistan, meanwhile, made history by defeating hosts Bangladesh 1-0 in the other semifinal. Abdul Samad Arshad broke the deadlock with a late winner in the 86th minute to send Pakistan into their maiden SAFF final.
The victory marked another significant milestone in a remarkable year for Pakistan football, as they now stand just one win away from claiming their first regional title.
The traditional rivals have already met once in this edition, with India securing a 3-2 victory in their opening Group B encounter on November 5. India established a commanding 3-0 lead through a brace from Suhail Ahmad Bhat and a goal from Manglenthang Kipgen before Pakistan scored twice in stoppage time to make the contest considerably closer.
Pakistan's disciplined defensive display against Bangladesh, despite facing sustained pressure from the hosts, will provide them with confidence heading into the title-deciding encounter.

item.title: Ackerman leads South Africa fightback after Hasan strikes
item.description:
Marques Ackerman struck his maiden Test century to lead South Africa's fightback against Bangladesh, despite Hasan Mahmud's impressive bowling, as the hosts reached 287-4 at stumps on Day 2 of the first Test at the Wanderers Stadium in Johannesburg today.
Ackerman made 157 off 164, smashing 21 fours and one six while Zubayr Hamza scored 83, helping South Africa recover from an early setback and cut Bangladesh's first-innings lead to 113 runs. The hosts had resumed their reply after Bangladesh were bowled out for 400.
Captain Temba Bavuma was unbeaten on 19, with Ryan Rickelton on 7 at the close.
The highlight of South Africa's innings was a commanding 202-run second-wicket partnership between Ackerman and Hamza, who steadied the innings after Hasan removed Aiden Markram in the second over.
Markram, who made 5, tentatively edged a scrambled-seam delivery from Hasan.
Ackerman and Hamza weathered some testing spells, remaining unbeaten throughout the second session despite sustained pressure from Hasan and Taskin Ahmed.
Taskin came close to dismissing Hamza, who was trapped leg-before, but the bowler had overstepped and the delivery was called a no-ball.
Ackerman looked increasingly assured and brought up his third consecutive fifty off 68 balls, whipping Mehidy Hasan Miraz through deep midwicket for four.
Hamza, after some early struggles, also settled into his innings, reaching his half-century off 82 balls with a single off Mehidy.
With his frontline bowlers struggling to break the partnership, Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto turned to Mominul Haque, and the move paid off.
Mominul ended Hamza's resistance with his left-arm spin, dismissing him for 83 off 129 balls, an innings featuring 12 boundaries.
Ackerman continued to dominate, reaching his maiden Test century off 125 balls with a single off Taskin. He then accelerated, putting Bangladesh's bowlers under further pressure before Hasan ended his innings at 157, having him caught by Taskin at backward square leg.
The dismissal also broke a 61-run partnership between Ackerman and Bavuma. Hasan struck again soon afterwards, removing Matthew Breetzke for 2 to prevent South Africa from taking complete control of the contest.
He also could have dismissed Ryan Rickelton, who edged a delivery behind, but Liton Das dropped the catch.
Earlier, Bangladesh resumed the day at 327-6 but managed only 73 more runs before being bowled out for 400.
Liton Das, who began the day on 89, completed his eighth Test century off 154 balls, pulling Marco Jansen to the fine-leg boundary.
Dane Paterson eventually dismissed Liton for 120 off 154 balls, an innings featuring 14 fours and a six. He became the second Bangladesh batter to score a century in the innings, following Towhid Hridoy's 137.
It was the first time two Bangladesh batters had scored centuries in the same Test innings against South Africa. Their efforts propelled Bangladesh to 400, their highest Test total on South African soil.
Paterson then cleaned up the tail, taking all four remaining wickets in the morning session to finish with figures of 4-92.
